title: Maximum Score Words Formed by Letters
statement:
You get a list `words`, a pool `letters` of single lowercase characters (a character may appear several times), and `score`, where `score[0]` is the value of `'a'`, `score[1]` the value of `'b'`, and so on up to `score[25]` for `'z'`.

Choose a set of words, using each `words[i]` at most once, that can be spelled together from the pool: every pool character spells at most one character of one chosen word, and leftover characters are fine. A set's score is the sum of the values of all characters in its words. Return the largest score any such set can reach (the empty set scores `0`).
constraints: words[i] and letters[i] contain only lowercase English letters
signature: int maxScoreWords(String[] words, char[] letters, int[] score)
notes:
## Intuition

There are at most 14 words, so at most `2^14 = 16,384` subsets: trying them all is affordable. Backtracking walks the same subsets as a binary decision tree (skip word `index` or take it) while keeping a running count of the pool's remaining characters. Taking a word subtracts its characters; if any count drops below zero, that branch is abandoned, so whole subtrees of impossible choices are never explored. Undoing the subtraction afterwards lets both branches share one `count` array.

## Approach

1. Count the pool: `count[c]` is how many copies of character `c` are in `letters`.
2. `backtrack(index, total)` decides words from `index` on, with `total` already scored. At `index === words.length`, update `best`.
3. First explore skipping `words[index]`.
4. Then subtract its characters from `count`, summing their values into `gained` and noting whether any count went negative (`fits`).
5. If it `fits`, explore taking it with `total + gained`.
6. Add its characters back so the caller sees the pool unchanged.

## Example 1, step by step

The pool has `a×2, c, d×3, g, o×2`. Values: `a=1, c=9, d=5, g=3, o=2`.

- `"dog"` scores 10, `"cat"` cannot fit (no `t`), `"dad"` scores 11, `"good"` scores 12.
- Taking `"dog"` and `"good"` needs three `o`s, so that branch fails.
- Taking `"dad"` (uses `d×2, a`) and `"good"` (uses `g, o×2, d`) needs `d×3`, which fits: `11 + 12 = 23`.
- `"dad"` with `"dog"` fits too, but only reaches 21. So `best = 23`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2^n · L): each of up to `2^n` branches processes a word of length at most `L`.
- Space: O(n) recursion depth plus the 26-entry `count`.

## Pitfalls

- Restore `count` after trying a word, even when it did not fit, or later branches see a wrong pool.
- A greedy choice by word value fails: in Example 2, `"xxxz"` is worth the most alone but blocks three words worth more together.
- Repeated letters inside one word (`"good"` needs two `o`s) must be counted individually.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | remaining copies of each character in the pool |
| `best` | highest score found for a complete choice |
| `index` | the word being decided |
| `total` | score of the words taken so far |
| `gained` | value of `words[index]` |
| `fits` | whether the pool still covers `words[index]` |
| `c` | character index, `0` for `'a'` to `25` for `'z'` |

narration.18: Use up one copy of this character.
narration.19: Add its value to the word's score.
